items.stem: Define the term 'start-up capital'.
items.answer: The finance needed to set up a business, for example to buy equipment, premises and initial inventory.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The finance needed to set up a business, for example to buy equipment, premises and initial inventory. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
items.answer: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that are used for several years, such as machinery; revenue expenditure is spending on day-to-day running costs, such as wages and materials.
items.markingKey: 1 mark capital expenditure; 1 mark revenue expenditure. [2]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why a business needs finance.
items.answer: To start up, buying premises, equipment and initial inventory; and to expand, for example by building a new factory or entering new markets; also for working capital.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Demand has grown faster than its small brewery can produce. Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd, a private limited company in South Africa with about 140 employees, brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. Explain why Cape Brew needs finance to launch alcohol-free craft beer.
items.answer: Points to develop for Cape Brew: businesses need finance for start-up, working capital and expansion; capital expenditure on equipment; working capital for extra inventory and receivables; promotion costs before revenue arrives.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: businesses need finance for start-up, working capital and expansion. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Cape Brew (beverages). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. capital expenditure on equipment; working capital for extra inventory and receivables. [3]

items.answer: Points to develop for Andean Coffee: businesses need finance for start-up, working capital and expansion; capital expenditure on equipment; working capital for extra inventory and receivables; promotion costs before revenue arrives.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: businesses need finance for start-up, working capital and expansion. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Andean Coffee (food processing). items.stem: The members are arguing about how much of the profit to reinvest. Green Valley Dairy Co-operative, a co-operative in India with about 80 employees, collects milk from 900 member farmers and makes yoghurt and cheese. Evaluate the importance of finance to the growth of Green Valley Dairy.
items.answer: For: finance needed for capital expenditure; working capital for larger operations; investment in new markets. Against: good management and marketing also needed; too much debt increases risk; growth can be funded gradually from profit. Judgement: for Green Valley Dairy it depends mainly on the speed of growth planned, and also on the cost of finance.

A top-level answer reaches a supported conclusion specific to Green Valley Dairy. [10]

items.stem: Define the term 'working capital'.
items.answer: The finance available for day-to-day operations: current assets minus current liabilities.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The finance available for day-to-day operations: current assets minus current liabilities. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a business can have too much working capital.
items.answer: Too much cash or inventory is idle: inventory has storage costs and cash could have been invested in assets that earn a return.
items.markingKey: 1 mark idle resources; 1 mark opportunity cost/storage costs. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways a business could reduce the length of its cash cycle.
items.answer: Hold less inventory, for example using JIT; and collect payment from customers faster, for example by offering discounts for early payment.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark method, 1 mark explanation): lower inventory, faster debt collection, longer supplier credit. [4]

items.stem: Blue Lagoon Tours is a partnership based in Nadi, Fiji. It runs boat trips and diving courses for tourists and employs about 14 people. Most customers book in the dry season and cash is short in the wet season. Explain how Blue Lagoon Tours could improve its working capital position.
items.answer: Points to develop for Blue Lagoon Tours: working capital = current assets − current liabilities; reduce inventory held; collect cash from customers faster; negotiate longer credit from suppliers.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: working capital = current assets − current liabilities. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Blue Lagoon Tours (tourism). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. reduce inventory held; collect cash from customers faster. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'liquidity'.
items.answer: The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between cash and profit.
items.answer: Profit is revenue minus costs over a period; cash is the money actually received and paid. Credit sales and purchases, loans and capital spending mean they differ.
items.markingKey: 1 mark profit; 1 mark cash; 1 mark example of difference. [3]

items.stem: Explain why liquidity is important for a business.
items.answer: Without enough cash to pay suppliers, workers and lenders on time, a business may be forced to close even if it is profitable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark pay short-term debts; 1 mark consequence of illiquidity. [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Han River Games: liquidity is the ability to pay short-term debts; suppliers and staff must be paid on time; lack of cash may stop production; creditors may force the business into liquidation.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why new businesses often fail.
items.answer: Poor cash-flow management means they run out of cash to pay debts; and lack of market research means demand is lower than expected.
